frameworks.name: Hook-Meat-CTA Ad Structure
frameworks.definition: Every paid ad has three mandatory parts: a hook (call-out that makes the viewer think 'this is for me'), meat (value = more good stuff or less bad stuff), and a call to action (offer + clear next step).

frameworks.name: Value Equation Reversal
frameworks.definition: Frame ad value by maximizing four good-stuff vectors (fast, easy, risk-free, likely) and minimizing four bad-stuff mirrors (slow, hard, risky, unlikely); each vector can also be sold as 'what you lose by not buying' to create a second set of copy angles.

frameworks.name: Levels of Awareness Ad Targeting
frameworks.definition: Eugene Schwartz's five-level model (unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware, most-aware) determines hook style: colder audiences need curiosity hooks with no solution reference; warmest audiences need only an offer restatement.

frameworks.name: Same Bundle Different Wrapper
frameworks.definition: Once an offer is proven to convert, keep the bundle identical but cycle through seasonal or event-based wrappers (holiday, Super Bowl, spring, back-to-school) to create perceived novelty without rebuilding the offer.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the us-versus-them ad strategy is best employed by non-market-leaders (underdogs) and should be avoided by the market leader, who should instead use us-versus-the-alternative (e.g., 'us vs. your couch') if they want contrast framing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: advertiser is NOT the market leader in their category
claims.mechanism: The market leader invoking a named competitor elevates that competitor; contrast against a behavior or lifestyle alternative avoids legitimizing rivals while still capturing the emotional contrast.
bounded_by: Market leaders should not use brand-name us-versus-them contrast

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in branding, negative associations occur automatically and are unavoidable: if an ad is structured so that most of its runtime focuses on an unappealing comparison object (e.g., chunky milk), audiences will associate the brand itself with that unappealing thing rather than the intended contrast.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: The brain cannot suppress a named image; instructing someone not to think of something forces the association. Ad runtime dominates association weight, so whichever object occupies more screen time gets paired to the brand.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for the warmest (most-aware) audiences, the optimal ad is simply a direct offer restatement with no curiosity hook required, because the audience's existing familiarity with the brand replaces the need to earn attention.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: audience is already familiar with the brand or spokesperson
targeting is set to warm or retargeted segments
claims.mechanism: Warmest audiences have already passed through problem-aware and solution-aware stages; additional hook content is wasted attention, and a clean offer converts faster.
bounded_by: Cold or unaware audiences require curiosity hooks that omit product references entirely

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that retargeting creatives can remain unchanged far longer than top-of-funnel creatives because the retargeting audience bucket refills continuously with new entrants, whereas top-of-funnel audiences see the same ads repeatedly and experience fatigue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: running a retargeting campaign separate from top-of-funnel campaigns
claims.mechanism: Retargeting pools are replenished by users who newly cross the trigger threshold (site visit, video watch percentage); the pool composition changes even if the ad does not. Top-of-funnel pools are static large audiences who see the same ad repeatedly.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that longevity of an ad in an active campaign is the most reliable proxy for that ad's conversion performance: if an ad is still running after months or years despite its content being stale, that is strong evidence it is generating positive ROI.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: ad is in a competitively managed paid campaign (not abandoned)
claims.mechanism: Advertisers cut ads that lose money and extend ad spend on ads that return positive ROAS; therefore survival time in an active spend environment is a revealed-preference signal of effectiveness.
bounded_by: Does not apply to organic posts or unpaid content which may survive due to neglect

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the biggest conversion gains on a paid traffic landing page come from reducing page load time, not from redesigning copy or layout, citing Neil Patel's research at approximately 2.5% conversion improvement per second saved in load time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: page load time is currently above 3 seconds

numbers.axis: page load time vs. conversion rate lift

anchors.value: ~2.5% conversion improvement per second saved (Neil Patel data, cited by Hormozi)

bounded_by: Effect diminishes once load time is already under 3 seconds

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that adding a second CTA button to a single-CTA landing page will increase conversions, and adding a third will likely also increase conversions; beyond that point, too many CTAs create confusion and reduce conversion.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: page currently has only one CTA button
claims.mechanism: Additional CTA buttons intercept visitors at different scroll depths who would have otherwise left without acting.

numbers.axis: number of CTA buttons on page vs. conversion direction

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that including an FAQ section at the bottom of a sales page will increase conversion because each FAQ item resolves the purchase objections of a small percentage of visitors who would otherwise leave unconverted.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: product has common objections that cannot be woven into the main copy without losing other readers
claims.mechanism: FAQs quarantine low-prevalence objections at the bottom so they do not disrupt the main narrative for the majority, while still resolving those concerns for the minority who have them.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the middle tier in a three-tier pricing structure should be positioned close to the tier the business wants most customers to choose: placing the middle price close to the top tier nudges buyers toward the top tier ('for a little more I get a lot more'), while placing it close to the bottom tier nudges buyers toward the middle tier.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: three-tier pricing with a small, medium, and large option
claims.mechanism: Customers evaluate price tiers relatively, not absolutely; the middle tier serves as a cognitive anchor that makes the adjacent tier look like the obvious best value depending on price gap placement.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for a buy-X-get-Y offer, a structure where the customer gets more free units than paid units (e.g., buy 1 get 2, or buy 2 get 4) will typically convert better than a mirror-structure (e.g., buy 3 get 3) because the perceived gap between cost and gain is larger.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: offer is structured as a buy-X-get-Y promotional format
claims.mechanism: Perceived value is driven by the ratio of what is paid versus what is received; a non-mirror structure (buy 1 get 2) makes the free portion feel disproportionate and anchors the perceived discount higher.

numbers.axis: ratio of paid units to free units in BOGO-style offer

anchors.value: expected higher conversion; also costs business less per conversion

bounded_by: Untested claim; Hormozi recommends split-testing to confirm

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that showing cancellation terms and procedures before a purchase increases conversion rather than reducing it, because it reverses the perceived risk of being locked in.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: product has a commitment period or cancellation complexity that prospects fear
claims.mechanism: Purchase hesitation in subscription or commitment products is partly driven by fear of being trapped; transparently showing the exit path removes that fear, making the purchase feel lower-risk.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that user-generated content (UGC) ads should be the backbone of any business's paid advertising because they provide effectively unlimited creative variety at low cost and can be generated by customers rather than requiring a production budget.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Customer-generated creative leverages the entire existing customer base as an ad production team; output scales with customer count, not with production budget.
bounded_by: High-ticket B2B products may require higher-production or founder-led creative to maintain brand authority

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that ads mimicking currently trending organic viral formats will convert better because they look less like advertisements, and the less an ad looks like an ad, the better it converts in general.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Pattern interruption works in reverse for native-looking content: viewers who have developed ad-blindness do not trigger their skip reflex when the content matches the aesthetic of organic posts they voluntarily consume.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that reading public ad comment sections is the lowest-cost method for discovering the most prevalent purchase objections from prospects (not customers), and that subsequent ad batches should include rebuttals to the highest-frequency objections first.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a brand spokesperson's personal audience trust and familiarity is the primary driver of above-par advertising return for branded ads, and that replacing the spokesperson with an unknown mascot will reduce performance even if the messaging is otherwise identical.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: ads rely primarily on spokesperson recognition rather than product demonstration
claims.mechanism: Audience familiarity with a spokesperson functions as a pre-built trust transfer; removing the known face removes the trust transfer mechanism, requiring the ad to re-earn attention from scratch via hook alone.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for email follow-up sequences targeting non-purchasers, each email should address exactly one objection ranked by prevalence (most common concern first), rather than bundling multiple objections in a single email.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: email sequence targets prospects who opted in but did not purchase
claims.mechanism: Bundling objection rebuttals dilutes each rebuttal and makes the email feel defensive; single-objection emails allow readers who share that specific concern to feel directly addressed.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for physical products and low-ticket e-commerce, image-heavy emails convert better, while for complex services or high-ticket products, plain-text emails resembling personal correspondence convert better, including superior deliverability.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: email sent to a prospect who has not yet purchased
claims.mechanism: Visual emails signal mass marketing, which reduces trust in high-consideration purchases; plain-text emails pass spam filters more easily and trigger a 1:1 correspondence heuristic that raises perceived credibility.
bounded_by: E-commerce and physical products are the exception where visual emails outperform

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that scarcity (limited quantity) and urgency (limited time) are distinct mechanisms that can be combined but should not be used interchangeably, because they activate different purchase motivations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that birthday and anniversary personalized offers provide a reliable monthly conversion lift because at any given month, one-sixth of the audience (one-twelfth for birthdays plus one-twelfth for anniversaries) is receiving a personally timed, higher-urgency offer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business has email contact with customer base and can trigger date-based personalized sends
claims.mechanism: Birthday and anniversary triggers create genuine individualized urgency for each recipient; collectively they fire continuously across the calendar, providing a steady drip of high-converting sends.

numbers.axis: proportion of audience receiving a date-triggered personalized offer in any given month

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that building a customer-driven ad generation loop within the business itself is superior to relying on internal production, targeting a ratio where customers generate roughly 80-90% of ad creative and the business generates only 10-20%.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: business has an existing customer base willing to generate public content

numbers.axis: share of ad creative by source

examples.text: Mint Mobile's Ryan Reynolds 'angry goat' ad (30-second format) uses a contrarian hook ('we do the opposite of big wireless'), an us-versus-them value contrast ('they charge you a lot, we charge you a little'), weaves humor throughout via a lower-back tattoo joke and a goat payoff instead of the promised 'happy customer,' and closes with a clear CTA to mintmobile.com plus the $15/month unlimited offer. Hormozi uses this ad as the canonical example of a fundamentally sound three-part Hook-Meat-CTA structure for an underdog brand.

Mint Mobile ran a campaign featuring a character called the 'Minty Fox' mascot alongside a chunky-milk analogy, positioning Mint as smooth milk versus competitors' chunky milk. The campaign underperformed. Hormozi attributes the failure to two errors: removing Ryan Reynolds (the known trust anchor) and structuring the ad such that most of the runtime was occupied by the repulsive chunky milk image, which caused audiences to associate the Mint Mobile brand with something disgusting rather than with quality. This is Hormozi's primary live example of how branding works through unavoidable association, not conscious messaging.

Mint Mobile's retargeting ad (running for approximately five to six years as of the analysis date) features basic text and a simple offer restatement with no Ryan Reynolds, no humor, and minimal creative. Hormozi argues this 'boring' ad's longevity is strong evidence it converts well within retargeting pools, because advertisers cut losing ads. He explains this as consistent with the most-aware targeting principle: retargeting audiences need only an offer restatement, not a full hook.

Mint Mobile ran a UGC-style ad featuring an unsponsored-appearing male reviewer who edified himself as a bargain-hunter ('I'm that guy'), disclosed the $45 upfront cost (3 months x $15), addressed the biggest budget-provider fear (will there be signal?), and closed with a CTA. Hormozi uses this as the model for a correctly sequenced UGC ad: hook via self-identification of avatar, edification of reviewer credibility, offer with real price, objection addressed ('less bad stuff'), benefit restated ('more good stuff'), CTA.

Mint Mobile's holiday Ryan Reynolds ad was shot using $500 stock footage, deliberately cheap-looking, with Ryan Reynolds explicitly calling out that they don't waste money like big wireless. Hormozi notes this is an example of brand message and ad production quality being aligned: a budget brand spending extravagantly on ad production would contradict the value proposition, while cheap production reinforces it.

Mint Mobile ran the same core offer (three months of unlimited at $15/month) across multiple seasonal wrappers: holiday, Super Bowl, spring, summer, and back-to-school versions. Hormozi frames this as the Same Bundle Different Wrapper framework and uses the analogy of a fraternity party planner who invents reasons for parties ('John got his wisdom teeth pulled, kegger') to illustrate that customers respond to the reason as novelty even when the underlying offer is unchanged.

Mint Mobile's landing page features a countdown timer visible above the fold, a moving banner CTA, multiple CTA buttons at different scroll depths, a zip code coverage checker that handles the primary purchase objection (service quality in my area), three pricing tiers (3-month, 6-month, 12-month), and an FAQ at the bottom. Hormozi walks through each element to illustrate how the page structure mirrors the top-of-funnel ad strategy: urgency above fold, offer restated in bold, objection resolution mid-page, FAQ at the bottom for residual concerns.

Mint Mobile's three-tier pricing page (3 months at $15 intro then $30/mo; 6 months at $35 intro then higher; 12 months at $15/mo flat) is analyzed by Hormozi as a pricing nudge toward the 12-month plan: the 6-month mid-tier is priced close to the 12-month tier, making the 12-month the obvious best-value choice by comparison. He uses the soda-size movie theater analogy to illustrate: when small=10oz at $5, medium=15oz at $9, large=20oz at $10, buyers see the large as obviously the best deal.

practices.text: When writing ad copy, begin by sorting your value proposition into two buckets: 'more good stuff' (faster, easier, more likely, less risk) and 'less bad stuff' (removes slowness, hardness, risk, uncertainty). Then create a second pass on 'selling the don't': describe what happens if the prospect does NOT buy (more bad stuff accumulates, good stuff is never gained).

To identify which competitor ads are performing best, look up their account in the Facebook Ads Library and sort by longest-running active ads; the older the ad and still running, the more likely it is profitable.

Before raising prices or testing new offers, test buy-one-get-two and buy-two-get-four structures against mirror buy-X-get-X structures to find which perceived-ratio converts better at your price point.
Add a zip code or location coverage checker to the landing page of any service with geographic constraints; it converts a top objection into a micro-commitment step that advances consideration.

To make price feel smaller in copy, translate the monthly cost into an everyday equivalent the target audience already spends money on (e.g., 'less than two coffees a month'), and test multiple everyday equivalents against each other for different audience segments.
Test whether a spokesperson introduction hook ('Hey, it's [Name]') outperforms a product or problem hook when running ads to a warm or moderately aware audience.
Study Amazon product pages to learn persuasion page structure: headline, subhead, bullets above fold, social proof mid-page, FAQ at bottom, and multiple CTAs at different scroll depths.
